Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics

The taxation of capital is a widely debated topic in specialized literature, the main themes starting from the complex nature of capital to different evaluations of inequality, the theoretical validity of optimal fiscal results and how to approach the restrictions imposed by capital mobility, as well as the specifics of the countries analyzed. In this paper we propose to carry out a theoretical analysis of the tax treatment of household capital income among the EU member states (we refer to income from specific assets, capital gains, inheritances and donations/gifts), in this sense using mainly a descriptive methodology, by appealing to various bibliographic sources, mainly from foreign literature as well as the use of official documents of the fiscal entities of the respective countries.

sections.heading: The Troubled Distinction between Capital Gain and Ordinary Income
paragraphs: ### The Troubled Distinction between Capital Gain and Ordinary Income The Internal Revenue Code divides taxable gains and deductible losses into two classes: ordinary and capital. Broadly speaking, capital gains are taxed at preferential, lower rates. Ordinary losses, if deductible, may be deducted from any taxable income, but only in certain circumstances. Capital losses are deductible from only a limited segment of income, and may be carried forward indefinitely.

[[S1|The Yale Law Journal]] The favorable consequences of capital gain taxation and the mixed consequences of capital loss treatment motivate taxpayers to seek "capital" or "ordinary" treatment as their interests dictate. The Treasury's interest in maximizing revenue conflicts with the taxpayers' desire to minimize taxes, and thus encourages the government to oppose the taxpayers' efforts. The resulting controversy has placed much pressure on the "capital"-"ordinary" dichotomy. The Code effects the division between capital and ordinary gain or loss by prescribing "capital" treatment for the gains and losses arising on the "sale or exchange" of "capital assets," which are described as a limited class of property: it thus requires a particular kind of transaction in a particular type of property to qualify for capital treatment.

For The Troubled Distinction between Capital Gain and Ordinary, [[S1|The Yale Law Journal]] The "sale or exchange" requirement can be interpreted in relation to sections 1001, which outlines the method of computing gain or loss on the "sale or other disposition of property," and 61(a)(3), which brings "gains derived from dealings in property" into gross income. For The Troubled Distinction between Capital Gain and Ordinary, these provisions apply only to transactions that "close out" the taxpayer's ownership interest in the property involved. Capital assets is defined as "property held by the taxpayer" which does not fit within five exclusionary categories. By and large, the exclusionary categories include: (1) property held for sale in the ordinary course of business; (2) property held for investment; (3) property held for use in a trade or business; (4) property held for use in a business or commercial activity; and (5) property held for use in a personal service activity.

sections.heading: Critique of Current Congressional Capital Gains Contentions
paragraphs: ### Critique of Current Congressional Capital Gains Contentions [[S2|The William Mary Law School Scholarship]] In recent years, the debate over capital gains has been dominated by the influence of the Republican Party, particularly the House Ways and Means Committee Chair, Bill Archer, R-Tex. Archer, while a minority member of the House Ways and Means Committee, sponsored income tax cuts for capital gains in 1978 and 1989. These tax cuts were intended to be brought about by indexing the basis of capital assets for inflation, either in conjunction with, or in lieu of, an exclusion of part of the gain realized upon a sale or exchange. Both proposals were passed by the then Democratic-controlled House, but were not passed by the Senate, and the proposals died in Conference.

[[S2|The William Mary Law School Scholarship]] The Senate Finance Committee Chair, Bob Packwood, R-Ore., when Chair in 1986, ended the 60% exclusion for long-term capital gains to partially pay for bringing the top permanent individual tax rate down from 50% to 28%. A 28% rate was also adopted as the top individual rate for capital gains. The Republican administration under President Bush attempted unsuccessfully from 1989 through 1992 to cut the individual capital gains rate 3 without raising the individual rate on ordinary income. Congress held hearings on and debated capital gains in 1989 and 1990.

Congress, with President George Bush's acquiescence, raised the top individual permanent rate on ordinary income to 31% in 1990, while maintaining the 28% ceiling on capital gains! This had the effect of restoring a capital gains preference at that rate, but limited only to individuals. [[S2|The William Mary Law School Scholarship]] The OECD taxation working paper, "Statutory tax rates on dividends, interest and capital gains," presents statutory tax rates on several forms of capital income, including dividends, interest on bonds and bank accounts, and capital gains on shares and real property, including integration between the corporate and personal levels. It updates the rates from an earlier tax working paper (Harding, 2013) and extends the analysis to consider the debt-equity bias of the tax system when the personal level of taxation is considered.

sections.heading: The Capital of the Households and Ways of Taxing It.
paragraphs: ### Sold a Property? Eight Different Ways to Reduce Taxes on Your Capital Gain [[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] When you sell a property, the tax implications can be complex. The capital gains tax is a significant financial consideration, and understanding how to reduce your tax burden is crucial. This article explores eight different ways to reduce your capital gains tax when you sell a property.

[[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] #### 1. **Capital Gains Tax on Property Sale** When you sell a property, you may be subject to capital gains tax. This tax is calculated based on the difference between the selling price and the original purchase price. The tax rate can vary depending on your income and the amount of capital gains you have realized.

[[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] #### 2. **Tax Deductions for Property Sale** You can deduct certain expenses related to the sale of your property, such as legal fees, appraisal fees, and closing costs. These deductions can lower your taxable income and, consequently, your capital gains tax. [[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] **Tax Deductions for Home Improvements** If you make significant improvements to your property, you may be able to deduct these expenses from your capital gains.

For example, if you replace your roof or fix major structural issues, you can claim these expenses as a deduction. [[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] **Tax Deductions for Mortgage Interest and Property Taxes** You can deduct mortgage interest and property taxes from your capital gains. This deduction is based on the amount of interest you paid on your mortgage and the amount of property taxes you paid on the property you sold. [[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] **Tax Deductions for Home Office** If you use your property as a home office, you can deduct the expenses related to your home office from your capital gains.

This deduction is based on the amount of expenses you incurred and the percentage of your total income that you used for home office purposes. [[S3|Journal of Financial and Monetary Economics]] #### 6. **Tax Deductions for Business Use** If you use your property for business purposes, you can deduct the expenses related to your business use from your capital gains. This deduction is based on the amount of expenses you incurred and the percentage of your total income that you used for business purposes.

sections.heading: Saving the Farm or Giving Away the Farm: A Critical
paragraphs: ### Saving the Farm or Giving Away the Farm: A Critical Analysis of the Capital Gains Tax Preferences [[S4|Digital USD University of San Diego]] The capital gains tax, a cornerstone of American tax policy, has long been a subject of heated debate. Critics argue that it has a detrimental effect on the economy, while proponents contend that it is necessary to maintain a balance between capital and income taxes. This article delves into the complexities of the capital gains tax, focusing on its impact on individual income taxes and the mechanisms that have been used to shift wealth to the wealthiest taxpayers. [[S4|Digital USD University of San Diego]] One of the primary concerns regarding the capital gains tax is its impact on the economy.

Critics argue that it distorts market signals and discourages investment, leading to a misallocation of resources. However, proponents counter that the tax has not generated more revenue due to tax policy, which has created policies that encourage holding capital property for long periods. [[S4|Digital USD University of San Diego]] Another significant issue is the inequities associated with the capital gains tax. When property passes through an estate, the inherent gain is completely eradicated, leaving the estate with no capital gains tax liability.

This creates a significant inequity, as it benefits the wealthiest taxpayers who can afford to hold onto their assets for generations. [[S4|Digital USD University of San Diego]] The article proposes several reforms to address these inequities and shift benefits towards the middle and lower class. One of the key proposals is to reallocate capital gains preferences, moving certain benefits towards the middle and lower class. This would involve phasing out certain preferences and eliminating those that only benefit the wealthiest taxpayers.

Another proposal is to eliminate the preferential treatment of capital gains, which would simplify the tax system and reduce complexity. [[S4|Digital USD University of San Diego]] The article also discusses the corporate taxation system, which has two principal policies: ordinary income is differentiated from capital gains, and the stockholder is distinguished from the corporation as a taxable entity. The article argues that these policies must be pursued vigorously if the two separate systems of taxation are to be maintained. However, the present system is inequitable and complex, and reform could eliminate many of the inequities and complexities.

sections.heading: Capital gains and surplus stripping
paragraphs: ### Sold a Property? Eight Different Ways to Reduce Your Taxes [[S6|cIRcle University of British Columbia]] When you sell a property, there are several ways to reduce your taxes. One common method is called "surplus stripping," which involves avoiding the second level of tax on corporate source income. This practice has been around since the 1926 revision of the Income War Tax Act, 1917, introduced to tax corporations and their shareholders.

However, changes in the Income Tax Act in 1977 limited the scope of surplus stripping operations, and subsequent legislation aimed to block perceived abuses. [[S6|cIRcle University of British Columbia]] Another method is "capital gains stripping," which allows individuals to defer tax on the appreciation of capital property. This is done by importing the abolition of capital gains tax at the corporate level, effectively providing unlimited deferral of tax upon the realization of appreciated capital property. While this method may not precipitate a serious loss of revenue, it undermines the principle of equity, a cornerstone of tax reform.

[[S6|cIRcle University of British Columbia]] In addition to these two methods, there are other ways to reduce your taxes when selling a property. One such method is "capital gains bailouts," which are established through the imaginative combination of statutory rules and results. These bailouts can provide individuals with unlimited deferral of tax upon the realization of appreciated capital property, making them a less long-standing problem for fiscal authorities compared to surplus stripping. [[S6|cIRcle University of British Columbia]] The government has only recently moved to eradicate capital gains avoidance with complicated and as yet untested legislation.

This new Canadian study deals with both surplus stripping and capital gains stripping, providing an interjurisdictional comparison of these avoidance activities and the corresponding efforts of fiscal authorities in Great Britain and the United States. [[S6|cIRcle University of British Columbia]] ### Theoretical Optimal Taxation of Capital [[S6|cIRcle University of British Columbia]] In advanced economies, the optimal tax treatment of capital is a topic of significant debate. This survey discusses how capital should be taxed, reviewing the theoretical optimal tax literature, surveying empirical studies on the distribution of capital and the distortionary costs of capital taxation, and analyzing the desirability of specific taxes on capital income, wealth, property, inheritances, and corporate profits. Our overall conclusion is that capital taxation plays an important role in an optimal tax system, but only certain ways of taxing capital are able to strike a balance between optimality and administrative feasibility.

paragraphs: ### Sold a Property? Eight Different Ways to Reduce Your Capital Gains [[S7|bepress Legal Repository]] When you sell a property, the tax implications can be complex. The capital gains preference, a policy that allows investors to defer paying taxes on gains from the sale of capital assets, can significantly reduce your tax burden. However, this preference has its drawbacks.

By eliminating the capital gains preference, you can reduce the complexity of your tax system and potentially lower your tax bill. [[S7|bepress Legal Repository]] The capital gains preference is a policy that allows investors to defer paying taxes on gains from the sale of capital assets, such as stocks, real estate, and collectibles. This preference is intended to encourage investment by reducing the immediate tax burden on investors. However, it has led to significant revenue loss for the government and has created a complex system of taxation.

[[S7|bepress Legal Repository]] The capital gains preference has been justified as a remedy for various problems, including inflation, bunching, lock-in, and double taxation. Inflation is a concern because it can erode the purchasing power of capital gains. Bunching refers to the practice of selling assets at a loss and then buying them back at a higher price, which can result in a loss of capital gains. Lock-in occurs when an investor holds onto an asset for a long time, resulting in a loss of capital gains.

Double taxation occurs when an investor is taxed on both capital gains and ordinary income. [[S7|bepress Legal Repository]] In the seventh section’s fifth paragraph, the first evidence point for Eliminating the Capital Gains Preference. Part II: The Problem of is that by eliminating the capital gains preference, you can reduce the complexity of your tax system and potentially lower your tax bill. This policy would also eliminate the "loophole" that benefits high-income persons, which has been a major source of complexity in the tax system.

The separation of the stockholder and the corporation as a taxable entity is premised on the distinction between ordinary income and capital gains. By eliminating the capital gains preference, that separation should fall with the demise of capital gains. [[S7|bepress Legal Repository]] In conclusion, the capital gains preference is a policy that has significant drawbacks. In the seventh section’s sixth paragraph, the second evidence point for Eliminating the Capital Gains Preference.

paragraphs: ### She Sold Her $1.8 Million Oakland Home at 56. California: The Old Property-Tax Assessment Follows Her Inland [[S3|24 7 Wall St]] In the bustling city of Oakland, California, a 56-year-old woman sold her $1.8 million home. This sale was not just a financial transaction; it was a significant event that left a trail of tax implications. The property tax assessment, which had been based on the old home's value, now follows her inland.

This situation highlights the complexities of property tax and the varying ways in which it is assessed and taxed. [[S3|24 7 Wall St]] The property tax assessment is a crucial aspect of local government revenue and is often based on the property's value at the time of purchase. However, as the woman's circumstances changed, her property's value decreased, leading to a discrepancy between the original assessment and the current market value. This discrepancy can have significant financial implications, as the old property-tax assessment follows her inland, meaning that she will now be responsible for paying property taxes on the lower value of her home.

[[S3|24 7 Wall St]] The situation underscores the importance of accurate and up-to-date property information. It also raises questions about the fairness of property tax assessments, especially when the value of the property changes over time. The woman's case highlights the need for regular reassessment of property values to ensure that property taxes are fair and accurate. [[S3|24 7 Wall St]] The tax treatment of household capital income among the EU member states is a topic of interest in specialized literature.

The paper proposes a theoretical analysis of the tax treatment of household capital income, including income from specific assets, capital gains, inheritances, and donations/gifts. The analysis uses a descriptive methodology, appealing to various bibliographic sources, including foreign literature and official documents from fiscal entities of the respective countries. [[S3|24 7 Wall St]] The paper's findings suggest that the taxation of household capital income is a complex topic with various theoretical perspectives. The EU countries analyzed in the paper have different approaches to the taxation of household capital income, reflecting the varying economic and political contexts of each country.
The paper's findings are valuable for policymakers and tax authorities, as they provide insights into the complexities of taxation and the need for a comprehensive understanding of the topic.
